claims.text: The starting material is a single-phase, disordered solid solution.
The starting material has moderate configurational entropy.
The starting material has no or weak low-temperature superconductivity.
Adding additional selected elements can raise the alloy's configurational entropy.
The added elements can raise configurational entropy without destabilizing the single-phase structure.
The relevant superconducting effect should occur primarily below about 10 K at ambient pressure.
Increasing atomic-scale compositional disorder produces enhanced local lattice distortions.
Increasing atomic-scale compositional disorder produces enhanced local potential fluctuations.
Higher configurational entropy stabilizes a disordered lattice configuration.
Entropy-induced disorder and lattice distortion alter the phonon spectrum.
Entropy-induced disorder alters local electron scattering.
The disorder-induced changes enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling strengthens pairing and produces a measurable superconducting transition.
The higher-entropy alloy should have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the baseline alloy.
The higher-entropy alloy should have a higher critical current density than the baseline alloy at low temperature.
The predicted improvement in critical current density is caused by enhanced electron-phonon coupling.
Very high configurational entropy or disorder can reduce superconducting performance.
Excessive disorder can localize charge carriers and thereby counteract beneficial electron-phonon coupling.
Constituent-element choice, mixing ratio, carrier concentration, and configurational entropy may impose an optimum rather than a monotonic entropy effect.
Samples processed identically and compared using resistivity, magnetic susceptibility, magnetization, and structural characterization can test the predicted superconducting differences.

contradictions.description: Phase separation is defined as outside the regime over which the hypothesis is expected to hold, but it is also treated as an outcome that falsifies the hypothesis. An out-of-domain sample does not by itself test the claimed mechanism.
